passage:
At the tea stall by the bus stop in their village, Shankar showed his cousin Lokesh a video on his phone. 'Look. They're saying the dam money was stolen by outsiders. It makes my blood boil.'
Lokesh, who taught at the block school, didn't argue about the dam. He asked, 'Who made it? Why does the music get louder there? Why does it end with "share before they delete it"?'
Shankar watched it again. It was true: the music swelled, the words came in red, the ending told him to share, not to check.
That weekend Lokesh showed him how the app picks what to show: the more you react, the more it sends. Shankar muted four angry channels. He followed the district newspaper and a farmers' radio show that interviewed people on different sides.
Next time a red-lettered video came up, he felt the heat rise and stopped. Built to make me angry, he thought. He scrolled past.

qa.q: What did the video say about the dam money?
qa.a: It said the dam money was stolen by outsiders.

qa.q: What was Shankar thinking when he stopped at the next red-lettered video?
qa.a: He recognised that the video was built to make him angry, and chose not to react.

qa.q: Which steps helped Shankar break the anger loop?
qa.a: Learning how feeds reward reactions, muting angry channels, following sources with more than one side, and pausing before reacting.

qa.q: How might Lokesh feel seeing his cousin scroll past such videos now?
qa.a: Lokesh may feel relieved and proud, having helped by asking questions rather than lecturing.

grounding: It shows a teen learning how feeds are built to provoke, muting rage channels, following varied sources and noticing anger-bait before reacting.

passage:
In the Izmir school library, the media studies teacher, Ms Kaya, put a post on the screen: a photo of a crowded bus with the caption 'THEY are taking over YOUR city. Share if you're angry!'
'Before you react,' Ms Kaya said, 'find three tricks.'
Zeynep, sixteen, felt her pulse tick up, and then made herself look. Capital letters. 'They' with no name. An order to share, no link to a source. Pablo, next to her, spotted a fourth: the photo was from another country, five years old.
That evening Zeynep went through her own feed. The more she'd clicked on angry posts, she realised, the more it had shown her. She muted six accounts that only ever posted outrage and followed two news sites that showed different sides of the same story.
On Friday a furious video popped up. Zeynep caught herself mid-thumb. Built to make me mad, she thought, and checked the source first.

qa.q: Where was the photo of the crowded bus actually from?
qa.a: The photo was from another country, five years old.

qa.q: How did Zeynep feel when she first saw the post, and what did she do with that feeling?
qa.a: She felt her pulse tick up with anger, then made herself slow down and look for the tricks.

qa.q: What skill did Zeynep build, and why is it useful?
qa.a: She learned to notice when a post is designed to anger before reacting, and to mute rage accounts and follow varied sources, so her feed stops steering her feelings.

qa.q: How might Pablo's discovery about the photo change how their classmates see such posts?
qa.a: It may make them more careful, realising how easily an old photo can be used to make them angry.

grounding: It shows a teen learning how posts and feeds are built to provoke, muting rage accounts, following varied sources and checking before reacting.

passage:
In the computer lab of their Guwahati school, Rekha ma'am projected a post onto the screen: a blurry photo, a red headline, and the words SHARE IF YOU'RE ANGRY.
"Before you react," she said, "tell me what this post wants from you."
Binita, who had shared one just like it last week, raised her hand slowly. "It wants me to be angry. And to share it before I check."
"How can you tell?"
"Capital letters. No source. The photo doesn't match the caption. And it tells me what to feel."
Rekha ma'am nodded. "Feeds learn from what makes you stop and react. Anger works best, so they show you more."
That evening Binita scrolled through her own feed and muted four accounts that only ever made her furious. She followed two news pages that showed different sides. Then she felt a new post rise in her chest like heat, and for once she just put the phone down.

qa.q: What words were on the post Rekha ma'am projected?
qa.a: SHARE IF YOU'RE ANGRY.

qa.q: How did Binita feel raising her hand slowly?
qa.a: She felt a little embarrassed, since she had shared a similar post the week before.

qa.q: Which of Binita's evening steps is most useful, and why?
qa.a: Muting the four rage accounts and following pages with different sides, because it retrains the feed away from constant anger.

qa.q: What might Rekha ma'am hope students take from the lesson?
qa.a: She hopes they learn to spot a post built to anger them before they react, which protects them online.

grounding: In a school lab a teen learns how feeds reward anger, then mutes rage accounts and follows balanced sources.

passage:
Hi Amandeep bhaiya,
Remember at Lohri when you took my phone, scrolled my feed and said, "This isn't news, this is a fight club"? I was angry at you for a week. Sorry.
I did what you said, though. I counted: of the first fifty posts, thirty-eight were people shouting about something. Then I tried your test. Before reacting to anything, I asked, "Is this post built to make me angry?" Most of them were. Same music, same red arrows, same "they don't want you to know".
I muted about twenty accounts. I followed a couple of pages that explain both sides, even when it's boring. And a science channel, because I actually like science.
It's weird. I'm less angry at home. Mummy noticed. I still get mad about real things, but now I check first.
Thanks for being annoying.
Yogesh

qa.q: How many of the first fifty posts were people shouting?
qa.a: Thirty-eight.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel when Amandeep first scrolled the feed?
qa.a: Yogesh felt angry and embarrassed, staying upset for a week.

qa.q: What question does Yogesh now ask before reacting, and why does it help?
qa.a: 'Is this post built to make me angry?' It creates a pause, so manipulation gets noticed before sharing or raging.

qa.q: How might Amandeep feel reading this email?
qa.a: Amandeep would likely feel pleased and touched that the advice was taken, and amused at being thanked for being annoying.

grounding: A teen learns to ask whether a post is built to provoke, mutes rage accounts and follows sources that show more than one side.

passage:
Sahil, you want to know why I stopped posting those clips? Honestly, one night I caught myself.
I'd seen this video, some guy screaming that "they" are taking our jobs, and my thumb was already on share. Then I thought of what our computer teacher said: if a post tells you exactly who to hate in ten seconds, somebody built it for that. So I didn't share. I looked up the numbers he quoted, and half were made up.
After that I went through my feed like a cleaning job. Muted anything that just made me boil. Followed two news pages that argue with each other, and a guy who explains economics without yelling. It's slower. Sometimes it's boring.
But I sleep better, and I'm not fighting my dad every dinner. I still care about jobs, bro. I just want the real version now. Imran's rule: angry post, stop, check, breathe.

qa.q: How many of the numbers in the video were made up?
qa.a: Half were made up.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling with his thumb on share?
qa.a: Imran felt a hot surge of anger, then a moment of doubt on remembering the teacher's warning.

qa.q: What does Imran's rule teach a friend like Sahil?
qa.a: Stop, check and breathe before reacting, since posts built to provoke rely on instant anger.

qa.q: How might Imran's dad notice the change?
qa.a: Imran's dad likely feels relieved and closer, now that dinners no longer turn into fights.

grounding: A teen notices a post built to provoke anger, checks it, mutes rage accounts and follows calmer sources with more than one side.

passage: I'm Pankaj, Pooja's older brother, so I sit across from her at dinner every night. For most of last term she'd scroll with this tight face and then read us some furious post about our town council. Then, after a computer class on how apps choose what you see, something changed. I saw her go through her follows one evening, tapping "mute" again and again. She said, "This guy posts the same outrage every day. It's built to make me angry." A few days later she was reading two news pages on the same council vote, one each side, and asking me which bits I believed. Last week a post about the council made her grip the phone. She put it down, went for water, and came back. I can't say what she felt inside. She just didn't share it.

qa.q: What did Pooja tap again and again one evening?
qa.a: She went through her follows tapping mute again and again.

qa.q: What does Pooja putting the phone down and going for water suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt a flash of anger but chose to pause and calm herself before reacting to a post designed to provoke her.

qa.q: What skill has Pooja built that Pankaj or others could learn from?
qa.a: She now notices when a post is built to anger her, mutes rage accounts and reads more than one side before deciding what to believe.

qa.q: How has dinner changed for Pankaj since last term?
qa.a: Pankaj no longer has to hear furious posts read out every night, and instead Pooja asks him what he believes, which feels more like a real conversation.

grounding: Shows a teen learning how feeds are tuned to provoke, muting rage accounts, following sources from more than one side and pausing before reacting.
